summaries.example: Imagine a toy block made from smaller pieces. If it is truly one single piece, it should not have separate parts. But if it has parts, it is not truly one. Śrīgupta used puzzles like this to question whether anything has a completely independent nature.
summaries.summary: Śrīgupta was a Buddhist philosopher from India whose dates are uncertain but who is generally placed around the seventh century. He developed an important Madhyamaka argument: anything with a completely independent nature would have to be either truly one thing or truly many things. He argued that neither option works. A single, partless thing cannot explain objects that have different parts, and a group of things would depend on the smaller things that make it up. So, nothing has an independent essence; this is called emptiness. Śrīgupta did not mean that nothing appears or functions. He described ordinary things as conventionally real: they depend on causes, work in expected ways, and seem satisfactory until we examine them very deeply. He also argued that enlightened understanding can include concepts, because teaching and helping people requires language.
key_ideas: Śrīgupta was an Indian Buddhist philosopher associated with the Madhyamaka tradition.
He argued that things are neither truly one nor truly many.
His argument was used to support the idea of emptiness.
He also said that ordinary things can still work and matter in everyday life.
He held that an enlightened person’s understanding can use concepts and language while still being fully accurate.
summaries.why_it_matters: Śrīgupta’s reasoning shows how a philosophical tradition can question the deepest structure of reality without saying that everyday life is meaningless. His work also connects questions about objects with questions about minds, mental images, knowledge, and teaching. The entry presents his views as part of debates within Buddhist philosophy, not as a settled answer accepted by everyone.

important_terms.definition: The idea that things do not have a completely independent, unchanging essence of their own.
A thing that has no smaller parts, either physical or understandable by careful thinking.
The view that things exist through connections with other things, rather than standing completely alone.
The everyday world as it appears and works for us, even though careful analysis shows that things are not independent.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be made of parts and still count as one thing?
Does something need to be completely independent in order to be real?
Can an idea be useful even if it is not the final truth?
Why might someone think that an enlightened person needs concepts to teach others?

summaries.example: Consider a smartphone. It appears to be one object, but it depends on a screen, battery, circuits, software, materials, makers, and conditions for its use. If we search for one completely independent core, we keep finding more dependence. If we instead say the phone is simply a collection of independent parts, we face the same problem: each part has spatial or conceptual divisions and depends on other parts. This illustrates the kind of analysis Śrīgupta uses, although his argument applies more broadly than to ordinary artifacts.
summaries.summary: Śrīgupta’s central contribution to Madhyamaka philosophy is his systematic use of the neither-one-nor-many argument. Madhyamaka defines an intrinsic nature as a kind of self-sufficient existence: a thing would exist, and be the kind of thing it is, independently of other things. Śrīgupta argues that anything with such a nature would have to be either a true unity or a true multiplicity. A true unity would be partless and independent. Yet material and mental items can be divided spatially, temporally, or conceptually. A true multiplicity would depend on true unities as its basic constituents, so it could not be independent either. Śrīgupta extends this reasoning to momentary and enduring things and to entities said to be omnipresent or localized. He also examines the relation between consciousness and mental representations, rejecting several realist and antirealist alternatives and arguing against a simple nondual awareness. The result is universal emptiness: nothing has an intrinsic nature. This is not nihilism. Śrīgupta describes conventional reality as dependent on similar causes, capable of causal or practical effects, and satisfactory only before ultimate analysis. Finally, he presents an unusual view of enlightened cognition: it can be conceptual while remaining veridical, since concepts and language are needed to guide others.
key_ideas: Śrīgupta gives a developed version of the neither-one-nor-many argument for emptiness.
The argument targets foundationalism: the idea that reality ultimately rests on independent, simple entities.
He applies the analysis to material objects, consciousness and mental representations, temporal entities, and omnipresent or localized entities.
His treatment of mind considers both realist and antirealist accounts of mental representations, as well as nondual awareness.
His three-part account of conventional reality combines dependence, causal efficacy, and satisfaction when not critically analyzed.
He argues that conceptual cognition need not be erroneous when it belongs to an enlightened knower.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry matters because Śrīgupta links metaphysics, philosophy of mind, epistemology, and the theory of two truths. His work appears to be an early synthesis of Madhyamaka metaphysics with the logical and epistemological tradition associated with Dignāga and Dharmakīrti. The neither-one-nor-many argument later became influential in Indian and Tibetan Madhyamaka debates, especially debates about whether consciousness or mental content could be ultimately real. His account also raises a lasting philosophical question: how can ordinary objects be dependent and empty while still supporting reliable action and communication?

important_terms.definition: In Madhyamaka, the absence of an intrinsic nature: nothing exists or is what it is with complete ontological independence.
A thing with no proper parts; Śrīgupta treats this as the strong metaphysical sense of being truly one.
A plurality whose basic members are true unities; its existence depends on those fundamental members.
The relation in which something depends on other things for both its existence and its being the kind of thing it is.
The study of parts and wholes, including whether a whole depends on proper parts.
Reality as it functions in ordinary experience: dependent, causally effective, and acceptable so long as it is not subjected to ultimate analysis.
The Madhyamaka framework distinguishing conventional truth from ultimate truth.
Śrīgupta’s claim that enlightened cognition may be conceptual, yet still invariably accurate and useful for teaching.

questions_to_think_about: Does rejecting fundamental simples really establish that nothing has an intrinsic nature?
Is a whole’s dependence on its parts different from its dependence on causes and conditions?
Can conventional reality be meaningful if it does not survive ultimate analysis?
Why does Śrīgupta think nondual awareness may be conceptually contradictory?
Could a cognition be both conceptual and completely accurate?

summaries.example: Think about a team project at school. You may call it “one project,” but it depends on several students, tasks, and materials. It is not one simple thing with no parts. It is also not an independent collection that exists without its members. Śrīgupta’s argument asks whether anything could be completely independent in this stronger way. He says that when we look closely, every candidate depends on parts, causes, or conditions.
summaries.summary: Śrīgupta was an Indian Buddhist philosopher associated with the Madhyamaka tradition. His best-known work develops the neither-one-nor-many argument, a method for defending emptiness. The argument starts with a strong idea of intrinsic nature: to have one, a thing would need to exist independently and be what it is independently of other things. Such a thing would have to be either a true unity or a true multiplicity. A true unity would have no proper parts. But anything extended in space, time, or thought can be divided or analyzed into parts. A true multiplicity would be built from true unities, so it would depend on them and could not be independent. Śrīgupta applies this reasoning to material objects, mental representations, consciousness, momentary and lasting entities, and things said to exist everywhere or only in one place. He concludes that everything is empty of intrinsic nature. He then explains how this conclusion does not erase the everyday world. Conventionally real things arise dependently, have causal efficacy, and satisfy ordinary expectations as long as they are not subjected to ultimate analysis. Śrīgupta also argues that enlightened cognition can be conceptual and still accurate, because teaching others requires language and concepts.
key_ideas: Śrīgupta’s main reasoning is called the neither-one-nor-many argument.
He challenges the idea that reality must rest on completely independent building blocks.
His analysis covers physical objects as well as minds and mental representations.
He considers both views that mental images are real and views that they are unreal products of error.
He argues that ordinary reality remains useful even though it lacks an intrinsic nature.
He gives a distinctive account of enlightened knowledge as accurate even when it uses concepts.
summaries.why_it_matters: Śrīgupta is important for showing how Madhyamaka connects claims about reality with claims about knowledge and mind. His arguments became influential in later Buddhist philosophy, including debates about consciousness and mental content. His account of conventional reality offers a way to distinguish “not ultimately independent” from “not real or useful at all.” His unusual position on conceptual enlightened cognition also challenges the simple contrast between concepts as mistaken and direct awareness as accurate.

important_terms.definition: A Buddhist philosophical idea that no thing has a permanent, self-sufficient nature that makes it exist entirely on its own.
A single, partless thing that would be independent of anything else.
A genuine many made from true unities; because it depends on those units, it is not fully independent.
Depending on other things for existence or for having the features it has.
The philosophical study of how parts make up wholes.
The everyday level of truth, where things appear, function, arise through conditions, and support ordinary activities.
The claim that a thing works as expected in practice or produces effects.
The Buddhist view that reality has no ultimate independent essence.

questions_to_think_about: If every whole depends on parts, can any whole be completely independent?
Can something be real in everyday life without being ultimately independent?
What problems arise if mental representations are treated as either fully real or entirely unreal?
Why might an argument about physical parts also apply to thoughts or moments of consciousness?
Does using language require conceptual thought?
